newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks sink on Wall Street spillover effect.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks sink on Wall Street spillover effect.

text.p: Tokyo stocks sank on Monday on what traders said was a spillover effect from Wall Street's second-largest points fall on Friday.
The dollar steadied against the yen and fell against the mark, as the market honed in on German interest rates ahead of the Bundesbank's decision on money market rates on Tuesday.
A smaller-than-expected rise in Japan's trade surplus for July announced earlier took the dollar higher against the yen, but comments by a U.S. trade official later offset the gains.
The stock market's benchmark 225-share Nikkei average ended down 284.93 points or 1.47 percent at 19,041.10. It briefly fell as low as 18,835.48 in the morning.
Nikkei September futures closed 440 points lower at 19,000.

Friday's plunge in the Dow Industrials dampened sentiment in a Tokyo stock market already bearish due to Japan's weak economic recovery, but the impact was limited by a view that the Dow's tumble was a natural correction after a long rally.
"I expect the effect from the tumble in New York to be limited, as it was a healthy correction after a long winning streak," said Hitoshi Morimura, chief portfolio manager at Meiji Life Insurance Co.
"Export-driven shares have been leading the market, but unless domestic demand-reliant issues generate a rally, the market overall is not likely to turn upward," he said.

The Dow lost 247.37 points to 7,694.66 on Friday, posting its biggest point drop since the 1987 stock market crash and the second-biggest point drop ever in a sell-off sparked by a weakening dollar and worries about corporate earnings.
In Tokyo, the dollar was driven down from a high of 118.05 yen on Monday on comments by a U.S. trade official.
Deputy U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) Jeffrey Lang told Reuters in Tokyo that the United States was concerned about Japan's trade figures.

Asked how concerned the USTR was by the nearly 70 percent rise in Japan's overall July trade surplus and the 35 percent rise in its surplus with the United States announced earlier on Monday, Lang said: "I haven't seen the trade figures this morning, but we are concerned."

The overall surplus came in at 849.08 billion yen ($7.25 billion), which was at the lower end of economists' forecasts, while the surplus with the United States grew 35.7 percent to 420.55 billion yen ($3.59 billion).
The U.S. currency stood at 117.40 yen and at 1.8120 marks in late afternoon Tokyo, compared with the New York closing levels of around 117.40 yen and 1.8190 marks on Friday.
"The dollar/yen tested both directions, but the dollar was unable to set a decisive trend in Tokyo," a Japanese commercial bank manager said. "People were looking at the mark."
Dealers said the dollar could face stronger corrective sales attacks against the mark depending on the Bundesbank's decision on interest rates.
The German central bank is expected to set the securities repurchase agreements (repo) rate on Tuesday and will hold a council meeting on Thursday after a four-week summer break.
Analysts said the Tokyo market was already vulnerable due to the weak state of the Japanese economy.
"The Japanese market is currently vulnerable to negative news because of the shaky recovery in the domestic economy," said Keiko Kondo, a strategist at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.
She said sentiment towards the economy has to improve before the Nikkei average can head higher.

Given the weakness of Japan's economic recovery after the consumption tax was raised in April and a payoff scandal involving top brokerages, the Nikkei 225 index may slip below last week's low of 18,801.68, analysts said.
On the Japanese bond market, the key September 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) futures contract ended firmer at 126.95, up from 126.83 at Friday's close.

The market initially rallied on falls in Tokyo stocks but later fizzled amid the summer holiday lull. Wall Street's dive had a limited impact on JGBs as short-end U.S. Treasuries firmed due to a flight to quality by investors, traders said. ($1=117 yen)
